questions.question_text:
Written in expanded form, $4^{3}\times 4^{2}$ is $(4\times4\times4)\times(4\times4)$.
Counting the factors, this equals which single power?

options.why: Multiplied the indices, $3\times2=6$, instead of counting the total number of factors.
Counted the five factors correctly but also multiplied the two bases, writing $4\times4=16$ as the base.
Made both slips at once: multiplied the bases to get $16$ and multiplied the indices to get $6$.

questions.question_text:
Expanding $3^{5}\div 3^{2}$ gives $\frac{3\times3\times3\times3\times3}{3\times3}$.
After cancelling, this equals which single power?

options.why: Added the indices as though the powers were being multiplied.
Counted the factors that were cancelled instead of the factors left over.
Multiplied the indices as in a power of a power.

questions.question_text:
Written in expanded form, $\left(5^{2}\right)^{4}$ is $(5\times5)\times(5\times5)\times(5\times5)\times(5\times5)$.
This equals which single power?

options.why: Added the two indices, $2+4=6$, instead of multiplying them.
Counted the eight factors correctly but also applied the inner index to the base, writing $5^{2}=25$.
Made both slips at once: evaluated the base as $5^{2}=25$ and added the indices to get $6$.

questions.question_text:
Expanding shows that a product of powers of the same base is one long string of equal factors.
Which statement completes the rule: when multiplying two powers with the same base, ...?

options.text: keep the base and add the indices
keep the base and multiply the indices
options.why: Uses the power-of-a-power rule, where the indices multiply, for a product instead.

options.text: multiply the bases and add the indices
options.why: Assumes each base is used again, but expanding shows the factors are all the same number.

options.text: add the bases and add the indices
options.why: Treats the product as if the whole expression, base included, were being added.

questions.solution_text:
$3^{2}\times 3^{4}$
$=(3\times3)\times(3\times3\times3\times3)$
$=3^{6}$
Keep the base and add the indices: $a^{m}\times a^{n}=a^{m+n}$.

questions.question_text: For which expression does expanding produce one string of identical factors, so the index law of multiplication can be used?

options.why: Adding keeps two separate amounts, so the factors cannot be joined and counted.
The bases differ, so the expanded factors are not all the same number.
Added an index for the factor $2$ as though it were another power of $6$, but $2$ is not a power of the base, so the expanded factors are not all the same number.

questions.question_text:
Written in expanded form, $3^{3}\times 3^{4}$ is $(3\times3\times3)\times(3\times3\times3\times3)$.
Counting the factors, this equals which single power?

options.why: Added the indices correctly but also multiplied the two bases, writing $3\times3=9$ as the base.
Multiplied the indices, $3\times4=12$, instead of adding them.
Made both slips at once: multiplied the bases to get $9$ and multiplied the indices to get $12$.

questions.question_text:
Write $\left(6^{3}\right)^{4}$ in expanded form.
Counting the factors, this equals which single power?

options.why: Added the two indices, $3+4=7$, instead of counting four groups of three factors.
Used the inner index $3$ as the number of groups, counting three groups of three factors instead of four.
Kept only the outer index and ignored the three factors in each group.

questions.solution_text:
$\left(6^{3}\right)^{4}$
$=(6\times6\times6)\times(6\times6\times6)\times(6\times6\times6)\times(6\times6\times6)$
$=6^{12}$
There are $4$ groups of $3$ factors, so $3\times4=12$.
